planting.note: Sow into gritty, sharply-drained soil once the ground has warmed, since this Altai and Siberian native resents wet winter feet far more than cold.

directions: Plant this low, clump-forming alpine in a rock garden or trough where its violet-blue, tubular flowers can be appreciated up close against the narrow silvery foliage. It wants full sun and lean, fast-draining soil, and resents summer humidity around the crown more than it minds cold winters. Deadhead spent flower spikes to tidy the mound and occasionally prompt a light rebloom. Established plants can be divided in early spring if a clump starts to open up in the center.

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings in spring into well-drained soil and give afternoon shade in hot-summer climates to prolong the winter-through-spring bloom.

directions: This long-cultivated Australian hybrid between Correa reflexa and Correa pulchella produces dusky pink-red, pendant bell flowers through the cooler months when hummingbirds and honeyeaters most need nectar. Grow it in gritty, sharply-drained soil, since correas are quick to sulk or rot in heavy, wet ground, and avoid high-phosphorus fertilizers that many Australian natives dislike. Light trimming right after flowering keeps the naturally dense, rounded habit neat without sacrificing next season's buds. It tolerates coastal wind and salt spray well, making it a dependable low hedge or border shrub in mild, frost-free gardens.

planting.note: Nick or soak the hard seed coat before sowing to break legume-style dormancy, then train young vines onto a trellis or fence as soon as they begin climbing.

directions: A vigorous Western Australian relative of the better-known Hardenbergia violacea, this twining vine smothers itself in sprays of purple-blue, pea-shaped flowers each spring, each bloom marked with a small yellow-green eye. It climbs readily over fences, arbors, or shrubs and tolerates poor, dry soils once established, making it a tough choice for difficult sunny banks. Prune back hard immediately after flowering to control size and encourage dense new growth rather than a bare, leggy base. It is drought-tolerant once rooted in but benefits from occasional deep watering through its first summer.
sources: Kings Park and Botanic Garden, Western Australia

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in coastal or sheltered inland sites, since the cream-edged leaves color best with some sun but the plant itself tolerates salt wind well.

directions: This cream-and-green sport of the glossy New Zealand broadleaf brightens hedges and screens that would otherwise be a solid wall of dark green. It takes clipping extremely well, making it popular for formal hedging in mild coastal gardens where the species thrives but often reverts partially variegated branches should be cut back to maintain the pattern. It shrugs off salt-laden wind and poor soil, which is part of why it became a staple seaside hedge plant in New Zealand and the UK. Give it full sun to keep the variegation crisp, since deep shade tends to wash leaves back toward plain green.

planting.note: Plant in a sheltered, frost-free coastal site in spring; this sport needs years of establishment before the crimson summer flower show matches the species.

directions: This cream-margined sport of New Zealand's iconic pohutukawa, the so-called New Zealand Christmas tree, pairs its crimson midsummer flower display with year-round variegated foliage interest. It is remarkably salt- and wind-tolerant, thriving right at the coastal edge where few other flowering trees survive, and it handles poor, rocky soil without complaint. Give it room to spread, since the species naturally develops a broad, gnarled canopy with age, and stake young plants against wind until roots anchor. Prune lightly after flowering only to remove any shoots that revert to solid green, which keeps the variegation dominant.

planting.note: Site in full sun near the coast where salt spray and reflected light intensify the cream-and-green marbling on the glossy leaves.

directions: Grown for its glossy, cream-marbled foliage rather than its inconspicuous flowers, this New Zealand coastal shrub earns the common name mirror plant from the high-gloss sheen on each leaf. It is tough in exposed, salt-blasted sites and sandy soil where many variegated shrubs fail, and it takes shearing well if used as an informal screen or container specimen. Pinch or prune young plants to encourage dense, bushy branching, since left alone it can become loose and leggy. Protect it from hard frost, as true freezing temperatures will damage or kill the foliage.

planting.note: Direct sow on lean, fast-draining soil after the last hard frost and withhold summer irrigation once seedlings are established, mimicking its chaparral habitat.

directions: A woolly-leaved California chaparral native, golden yarrow covers itself in flat-topped clusters of bright yellow flowers from late spring into summer, drawing in butterflies and native bees. It thrives on neglect, preferring rocky or sandy soil with little to no supplemental water once roots are established, and it rots quickly in rich, moist garden beds. Cut plants back by about a third after the main bloom flush to keep the subshrub compact and to encourage a second round of flowers. It pairs naturally with California sagebrush and buckwheats in a dry, low-water border.
